metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization rate measures the share of provisioned compute doing real work over time, not at peak. It is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.

The distinction between time and peak is the whole point. A fleet sized for its busiest hour will sit mostly idle the rest of the day, and idle servers still draw power, hold licenses, and depreciate. Utilization measured over time captures that gap. Utilization measured at peak hides it.

For AI specifically, this matters because accelerators are the most expensive capacity in the building. Provisioned compute that is not doing real work is paid for in power and capital either way. The metric sits in the capacity and server use category alongside stranded power and space per cabinet and floor loading limits, which are the physical constraints on how much compute a building can hold. Utilization is the operational counterpart to those limits: it says how much of the compute already installed is actually earning its keep.

The data does not give a target utilization rate, a current rate, or a breakdown by workload type. It defines the metric and places it in a category. It does not say how AI workloads differ from general enterprise workloads in utilization, and it does not connect utilization to any specific power or cost figure. Those connections would require data this page does not carry.
